More steps did **not** buy a better val_bpb here: steps 684 vs 632 (+8.2%) yet val_bpb 1.097067 vs 1.094760 (+0.002307 worse, inside the 2-sigma 0.005730 band).

Contrast with the same knob at width 512 (exp_tput_mlp_exp_2: 1.147892 -> 1.132007, -0.0159, KEEP). So the MLP 3->2 gain **did not transfer** to width 384. Two readings, both worth testing:

1. The width-512 MLP2 win was itself mostly a step-count effect (+12.5% steps); at width 384 the model is much smaller (28.3M vs 30.7M params) and +8% steps was not enough to overcome the lost MLP capacity.
2. There is a capacity floor: below width 384 / MLP3, cutting capacity starts to cost per-step quality at roughly the rate that extra steps gain.

This refines rather than refutes the "steps dominate" finding: steps dominate *while capacity is not the binding constraint*. AR48 (+46% steps, -33.5% params) was a large win; MLP2 on top (+8.2% steps, -7.7% params) was neutral-to-slightly-negative.

  re-scoped rather than defended.

**What changed the operating point (Step 1b2).** All three KEEPs were throughput KEEPs and all
three bought the same thing: more optimizer steps in the fixed 300 s budget (193 -> 374 -> 410
-> 433). The 2**18 KEEP won while processing FEWER tokens (98.0M vs 101.2M), so the response is

### The central contribution: step channel is dead, *unconfounded*

Seven clean paired "cheaper step" comparisons in `logs/experiments.jsonl`. The
two that change ONLY `TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE` (model unchanged, so no capacity
confound) are decisive:

| 2**18 -> 2**17 | 487 -> 956 | -0.043721 | -0.00454 |

632 steps. The saturation is a property of the base's step count, not of the
